kangaroo-at-2011-student-07.title: Height along the unrolled paper
kangaroo-at-2011-student-07.body:
Put the cylinder (radius $r$) upright and let $\theta$ be the angle around its axis. A plane cut has height $h(\theta) = h_0 + k\cos\theta$ — it rises and falls smoothly. Unrolling turns $\theta$ into the horizontal coordinate $r\theta$, so the edge of the paper becomes a **cosine curve**: one smooth hump with inflection points, flat-ish at the ends and no corners.

A and E have corners, B and D are arcs that meet the sides steeply (not wave-shaped). Only C is a smooth wave.

**Answer: (C)**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-08.title: Cut and rotate
kangaroo-at-2011-student-08.body:
Draw the perpendicular from $S$ to the line $QR$, with foot $U$. Then $STQU$ is a rectangle. Rotating triangle $STP$ by $90^\circ$ about $S$ moves $P$ onto $R$ (since $SP = SR$ and $\angle PSR = 90^\circ$) and $T$ onto $U$, so triangles $STP$ and $SUR$ are congruent and $SU = ST = 5$.

So $STQU$ is a $5\times5$ square, and the quadrilateral has the same area: $[PQRS] = [STQU] = 25$.

**Answer: (C) 25**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-08.title: Coordinates
kangaroo-at-2011-student-08.body:
Put $S = (0,5)$, $T = (0,0)$, $P = (-p, 0)$. Rotating $P$ by $90^\circ$ about $S$ gives $R = (5, 5-p)$. Then $Q = (5, 0)$ (since $QR \perp PQ$). Shoelace for $P(-p,0), Q(5,0), R(5,5-p), S(0,5)$: area $= \frac12\left|(-p)(0) - 5\cdot0 + 5(5-p) - 5\cdot0 + 5\cdot5 - 0 + 0 - (-p)\cdot5\right| = \frac12(25 - 5p + 25 + 5p) = 25$.

**Answer: (C) 25**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-09.title: Count and subtract
kangaroo-at-2011-student-09.body:
There are $\frac{2011+1}{2} = 1006$ odd numbers. The odd multiples of 3 are $3\cdot1, 3\cdot3, \dots, 3\cdot 669$ (the largest odd $m$ with $3m \le 2011$ is 669), i.e. $\frac{669+1}{2} = 335$ numbers. Remaining: $1006 - 335 = 671$.

**Answer: (C) 671**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-09.title: Residues mod 6
kangaroo-at-2011-student-09.body:
Odd numbers not divisible by 3 are those $\equiv 1$ or $5 \pmod 6$. From 1 to 2010 there are 335 complete blocks of 6, each giving 2: 670. Then 2011 $\equiv 1 \pmod 6$ adds one more: 671.

**Answer: (C) 671**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-10.title: Set the probabilities equal
kangaroo-at-2011-student-10.body:
With $n$ dice: $P(\text{no six}) = \frac{5^n}{6^n}$ and $P(\text{exactly one six}) = \frac{n\cdot 5^{n-1}}{6^n}$. Equal means $5^n = n\cdot5^{n-1}$, i.e. $n = 5$.

**Answer: (B) 5**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-11.title: Case analysis
kangaroo-at-2011-student-11.body:
When three rectangles form a rectangle, one of them runs along a whole side of it, and the other two together form a rectangle as well.

- **The $7\times11$ runs along a whole side.** The rest has a side of length 11 or 7, split into two pieces of equal width.
  - Side 11: $11 = 8 + 3$ with width 4 gives a third rectangle $3\times4$; $11 = 4 + 7$ with width 8 gives $7\times8$.
  - Side 7: $7 = 4 + 3$ with width 8 gives $3\times8$.
- **The $4\times8$ runs along a whole side.** The rest has a side 8 (or 4); $8 = 7 + 1$ with width 11 gives $1\times11$ (the side 4 is too short for the $7\times11$).
- **The third runs along a whole side.** Then $7\times11$ and $4\times8$ alone would have to form a rectangle, which is impossible (no common side length).

Possible third rectangles: $3\times4$, $7\times8$, $3\times8$, $1\times11$. The largest is $7\times8$ (area 56; the whole rectangle is then $15\times11$).

**Answer: (D) 7 by 8**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-12.title: Everything in terms of the centre
kangaroo-at-2011-student-12.body:
The edge-middle cells hold 2 (top), 1 (left), 3 (right), 4 (bottom). Call the centre $e$. Each $2\times2$ square contains one corner, two edge cells and the centre:

- top-left: corner $= 10 - 2 - 1 - e = 7 - e$,
- top-right: $10 - 2 - 3 - e = 5 - e$,
- bottom-left: $10 - 1 - 4 - e = 5 - e$,
- bottom-right: $10 - 3 - 4 - e = 3 - e$.

The five remaining numbers sum to $e + (7-e) + (5-e) + (5-e) + (3-e) = 20 - 3e$. With $e$ a whole number this is $2 \pmod 3$: possible values are $\dots, 11, 14, 17, 20, \dots$. None of 9, 10, 12, 13 is of this form.

**Answer: (E)**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-13.title: Group into families
kangaroo-at-2011-student-13.body:
- 6 children with exactly one sibling: families of 2, so $6/2 = 3$ families.
- 9 children with two siblings: families of 3, so $9/3 = 3$ families.
- 4 children with three siblings: one family of 4.
- The other $48 - 6 - 9 - 4 = 29$ children come alone: 29 families.

Total $3 + 3 + 1 + 29 = 36$.

**Answer: (D) 36**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-14.title: Identify the branches
kangaroo-at-2011-student-14.body:
The sketch consists of four curves leaving the origin with a vertical tangent: up-right, down-right, up-left and down-left, passing through $(1,1)$, $(1,-1)$, $(-1,1)$, $(-1,-1)$. These are the graphs of $\sqrt{x}$, $-\sqrt{x}$, $\sqrt{-x}$ and $-\sqrt{-x}$. The graph of $\sqrt{|x|}$ is the union of the first and third, and $-\sqrt{|x|}$ the union of the second and fourth, so they are included too: 6 graphs.

The parabolas $y = \pm x^2$ are not included: they have a horizontal tangent at the origin.

**Answer: (D) 6**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-15.title: Isosceles triangle
kangaroo-at-2011-student-15.body:
Let $J$ be the joint and $T$ the tip of the blade. The right edge of the cleaned area is the blade $JT$ in its extreme position, and the upper edge is the arc traced by $T$, a circle about $O$; its tangent at $T$ is perpendicular to $OT$.

Triangle $OJT$ is isosceles ($OJ = JT$) with apex angle $\alpha$ at $J$, so $\angle OTJ = \frac{\pi-\alpha}{2}$.

The angle $\beta$ inside the cleaned area is between $TJ$ and the tangent on the far side of $TO$: $\beta = \angle JTO + \frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{\pi - \alpha}{2} + \frac{\pi}{2} = \pi - \frac{\alpha}{2}$.

**Answer: (B) $\pi - \frac{\alpha}{2}$**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-16.title: Strip widths
kangaroo-at-2011-student-16.body:
A parallelogram cut out by two strips of widths $p$ (horizontal strip) and $q$ (sloped strip) has area $\frac{pq}{\sin\varphi}$, where $\varphi$ is the angle between the two directions.

Circle $X$ (radius $R$) touches the bottom two horizontal lines and the left two sloped lines, so both of those strips have width $2R$. Circle $Z$ (radius $\rho$) shows that the upper horizontal strip and the right sloped strip have width $2\rho$.

- Parallelogram $Y$ lies in the lower horizontal strip ($2R$) and the right sloped strip ($2\rho$): $Y = \frac{4R\rho}{\sin\varphi}$.
- Parallelogram $T$ lies in the upper horizontal strip ($2\rho$) and the left sloped strip ($2R$): $T = \frac{4R\rho}{\sin\varphi}$.

So $T = Y$: knowing just one area (namely $Y$) is enough.

**Answer: (A) 1**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-17.title: Read off what the picture forces
kangaroo-at-2011-student-17.body:
The remaining piece of the parabola opens upwards and is still falling at $A$ (the lowest point is further right).

- Opens upwards: $a > 0$ — true.
- $y(1) = a + b + c = -10 < 0$ — true.
- The parabola opens up and takes the negative value $-10$, so it crosses the $x$-axis twice: $b^2 - 4ac > 0$ — true.
- Falling at $x = 1$: $y'(1) = 2a + b < 0$, so $b < -2a < 0$ — true.
- $c$: e.g. $y = x^2 - 20x + 9$ passes through $(1,-10)$, opens up, falls at $x=1$, and has $c = 9 > 0$. So $c < 0$ could be false.

**Answer: (E)**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-18.title: Equal tangent segments
kangaroo-at-2011-student-18.body:
From each vertex the two tangent segments to the circle are equal. Call them $a, b, c, d, e, f$ at $A, \dots, F$. Then $AB = a + b$, $BC = b + c$, ..., $FA = f + a$. Hence
$$AB + CD + EF = a+b+c+d+e+f = BC + DE + FA.$$
So $4 + 6 + 8 = 5 + 7 + FA$, giving $FA = 6$.

**Answer: (D) 6**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-19.title: Cancel, then bound
kangaroo-at-2011-student-19.body:
Cancelling $G$ and one $A$, the expression is $\frac{K\cdot A\cdot N\cdot R\cdot O^2}{M\cdot E}$, where $K, A, N, R, O, M, E$ (and $G$) are different nonzero digits.

**Value 1 is impossible:** the denominator is at most $9\cdot8 = 72$. If $O = 1$, the numerator is at least $2\cdot3\cdot4\cdot5 = 120$; if $O \ge 2$, it is at least $1\cdot3\cdot4\cdot5\cdot 2^2 = 240$ (or more). Either way numerator $>$ denominator.

**Value 2 works:** $O = 1$, $M\cdot E = 9\cdot8 = 72$, $K\cdot A\cdot N\cdot R = 2\cdot3\cdot4\cdot6 = 144$, and $G = 5$. Then the value is $\frac{144}{72} = 2$.

**Answer: (B) 2**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-20.title: Count the men
kangaroo-at-2011-student-20.body:
There are exactly 5 women. If there were 3 or more men, a group of 3 men and 3 others would contain at most 3 women — contradicting Günther. So there are at most 2 men. But Gerhard and Günther themselves are male members, so there are exactly 2 men and $5 + 2 = 7$ members. (Check: any 6 of the 7 members include at least 4 women.)

**Answer: (B) 7**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-21.title: Inclusion–exclusion
kangaroo-at-2011-student-21.body:
A number is divisible by both 6 and 7 exactly when it is divisible by 42. So the balls divisible by 6 or by 7 number $30 + 20 - 10 = 40$. There may be no other balls, so the minimum is 40.

**Answer: (B) 40**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-22.title: Sequences containing both (intended reading)
kangaroo-at-2011-student-22.body:
We want arithmetic sequences of positive integers that contain all terms of both sequences. The common difference $d$ must divide the difference of any two terms of the first sequence (so $d \mid 15$) and of the second ($d \mid 26$). Since $\gcd(15, 26) = 1$, $d = 1$: the sequence is $s, s+1, s+2, \dots$ and must contain 5, so $s \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$. That gives 5 sequences.

**Answer: (C) 5** (the official key also accepts E, see below)

kangaroo-at-2011-student-22.title: Sequences contained in both (literal reading)
kangaroo-at-2011-student-22.body:
The common terms satisfy $n \equiv 5 \pmod{15}$ and $n \equiv 35 \pmod{26}$, i.e. $n \equiv 35 \pmod{390}$: $35, 425, 815, \dots$. Every arithmetic sequence such as $35 + 390k$, $425 + 390k$, $35 + 780k, \dots$ is a subsequence of both — infinitely many. Because of this ambiguity the official answer key accepts (C) and (E).

**Answer: (C), also accepted (E)**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-23.title: Plug in numbers
kangaroo-at-2011-student-23.body:
Start with 2011: $\frac{1}{1-2011} = -\frac{1}{2010}$, then $\frac{1}{1 + \frac1{2010}} = \frac{2010}{2011}$, then $\frac{1}{1 - \frac{2010}{2011}} = 2011$. The values cycle with period 3: $f_1, f_4, f_7, \dots, f_{2011}$ all give 2011.

**Answer: (A) 2011**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-24.title: The total must be a square
kangaroo-at-2011-student-24.body:
With $r$ red, $g$ green and $n = r + g$ balls:
$$\frac{r(r-1) + g(g-1)}{n(n-1)} = \frac12 \iff 2(r^2 + g^2) - 2n = n^2 - n.$$
Using $2(r^2+g^2) = (r+g)^2 + (r-g)^2 = n^2 + (r-g)^2$: $(r-g)^2 = n$. So $n$ must be a perfect square; among the choices only $81 = 9^2$ (e.g. 45 red and 36 green).

**Answer: (A) 81**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-24.title: Check with the example
kangaroo-at-2011-student-24.body:
With 45 red and 36 green: same colour in $\binom{45}2 + \binom{36}2 = 990 + 630 = 1620$ of the $\binom{81}{2} = 3240$ pairs, exactly half. ✓

**Answer: (A) 81**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-25.title: Two equations
kangaroo-at-2011-student-25.body:
Let $F$ be the free allowance per passenger and $p$ the price per extra kg. The couple pays for $60 - 2F$ kg, Mr. Wander for $60 - F$ kg:
$$(60-2F)p = 3, \qquad (60-F)p = 10.5.$$
Dividing: $\frac{60-F}{60-2F} = 3.5$, so $60 - F = 210 - 7F$, $F = 25$ (and $p = 0.30$ € per kg).

**Answer: (D) 25**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-25.title: Check the choices
kangaroo-at-2011-student-25.body:
For $F = 25$: the couple pays for 10 kg (3 €, so 0.30 € per kg) and Mr. Wander for 35 kg: $35 \cdot 0.30 = 10.50$ €. ✓

**Answer: (D) 25**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-26.title: Split 100 = 4 · 25
kangaroo-at-2011-student-26.body:
$(x-9)(x+9) \equiv 0 \pmod{100}$.

- Mod 4: $x^2 \equiv 1$, so $x$ is odd.
- Mod 25: 5 cannot divide both $x - 9$ and $x+9$ (their difference is 18), so $25 \mid x-9$ or $25 \mid x+9$: $x \equiv 9$ or $16 \pmod{25}$.

Below 100: $x \in \{9, 34, 59, 84\} \cup \{16, 41, 66, 91\}$; the odd ones are 9, 59, 41, 91. Their sum is $200$.

**Answer: (A) 200**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-26.title: Symmetry
kangaroo-at-2011-student-26.body:
If $x$ works, so does $100 - x$ (since $(100-x)^2 \equiv x^2$). The solutions pair up as $9 + 91$ and $41 + 59$, sum $2\cdot 100 = 200$.

**Answer: (A) 200**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-27.title: List all multisets
kangaroo-at-2011-student-27.body:
The scores per arrow are 1, 3, 7, 12. Three arrows give $\binom{4+2}{3} = 20$ different multisets of scores. Their totals:

3, 5, 9, 14, 7, 11, 16, 15, 20, 25 (with at least one 1), and 9, 13, 18, 17, 22, 27, 21, 26, 31, 36 (without 1).

Only one coincidence: $1 + 1 + 7 = 3 + 3 + 3 = 9$. So there are $20 - 1 = 19$ different totals.

**Answer: (C) 19**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-28.title: Exponents of 2 and 3
kangaroo-at-2011-student-28.body:
Let $N = a^2 = 2b^3 = 3c^5$ with $N = 2^x 3^y \cdots$.

- Exponent of 2: $x$ even, $x \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, $x \equiv 0 \pmod 5$. Smallest: $x = 10$.
- Exponent of 3: $y$ even, $y \equiv 0 \pmod 3$, $y \equiv 1 \pmod 5$. Smallest: $y = 6$.
- Any other prime would need an exponent divisible by 30; leave them out.

$N = 2^{10}3^6$ gives $a = 2^5 3^3$, $b = 2^3 3^2$, $c = 2^2 3$, so $abc = 2^{10}3^6$ with $(10+1)(6+1) = 77$ divisors.

Any other solution has $x \ge 10$, $y \ge 6$ (the exponents satisfy the same congruences and the next solutions are $x = 40$, $y = 36$), so $abc$ has at least as many divisors.

**Answer: (D) 77**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-29.title: Which numbers are usable
kangaroo-at-2011-student-29.body:
Every cell has at least 2 neighbours, and each neighbour must share a prime with it.

If all numbers were $\le 25$: 1 cannot be used, and neither can 13, 17, 19, 23 (no other multiple $\le 25$), nor 11 (only 22 shares a factor, but 11 needs at least 2 neighbours). That leaves $\{2,\dots,25\}$ minus 5 numbers: only 19 numbers — too few. So $n \ge 26$.

With $n = 26$ the usable numbers are exactly 20: $2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9,10,12,14,15,16,18,20,21,22,24,25,26$. They can be arranged:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline 7&14&2&4&8\\\hline 21&6&16&22&26\\\hline 12&18&24&20&10\\\hline 9&3&15&25&5\\\hline\end{array}$$
(7 sits in a corner next to 14 and 21; 5 in a corner next to 10 and 25; all other neighbours share 2, 3 or 5.)

**Answer: (C) 26**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-30.title: Coordinates
kangaroo-at-2011-student-30.body:
Let the big cube be $[0,3]^3$; the plane is $x + y + z = 4.5$. The small cube $[i,i+1]\times[j,j+1]\times[k,k+1]$ ($i,j,k \in \{0,1,2\}$) has $x+y+z$ ranging over $[s, s+3]$ with $s = i+j+k$, so it is cut iff $s < 4.5 < s+3$, i.e. $s \in \{2, 3, 4\}$.

Counting triples from $\{0,1,2\}$: sum 2: 6, sum 3: 7, sum 4: 6. Total 19.

**Answer: (C) 19**

kangaroo-at-2011-student-30.title: Complement
kangaroo-at-2011-student-30.body:
Uncut cubes have $s \le 1$ or $s \ge 5$: sum 0: 1, sum 1: 3, sum 5: 3, sum 6: 1 — total 8. So $27 - 8 = 19$ are cut.

**Answer: (C) 19**
